course.title: Applied Ethics
course.description: A practical tour of moral reasoning that takes the major ethical frameworks — consequentialism, deontology, and virtue ethics — and puts them to work on real dilemmas in medicine, business, technology, and the environment. Structure adapted from OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: Applied ethics is best described as…
options: applying moral principles to specific real-world issues
the study of grammar in moral language
a set of laws every country must adopt
questions.explanation: Applied ethics takes normative frameworks and works out what they imply for concrete cases — see 'What is applied ethics?'.

questions.prompt: A theory that judges an action by its consequences is…
questions.explanation: Consequentialism locates rightness in outcomes — covered in 'Three frameworks as tools'.

questions.prompt: Kant's deontology says the rightness of an act depends mainly on…
options: the agent's duties and the principle behind the act
questions.explanation: Deontology judges acts by duty and maxim, not results.

questions.prompt: Virtue ethics asks primarily…
options: what a person of good character would do
questions.explanation: Virtue ethics centers character and flourishing rather than a single act-rule.

questions.prompt: In medical ethics, 'autonomy' refers to…
options: a patient's right to make informed decisions about their own care
questions.explanation: Autonomy is a core bioethics principle — see 'Bioethics'.

questions.prompt: 'Algorithmic bias' most directly concerns…
options: systems producing unfair outcomes for some groups
questions.explanation: Bias arises when data or design skew results against groups — see 'Technology & AI'.

questions.prompt: An argument that we owe moral consideration to future generations is central to…
questions.explanation: Intergenerational duty is a recurring environmental-ethics theme.

questions.prompt: Rawls's idea of choosing rules behind a 'veil of ignorance' is a tool for thinking about…
questions.explanation: The veil of ignorance models impartial fairness — see quizzes and project.

lessons.title: Three frameworks as decision tools
lessons.grammar_note: Frameworks are lenses, not switches — the same case can look different through each.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain consequentialism, deontology, and virtue ethics, and use each as a distinct tool for analyzing a dilemma. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which framework judges an act by its *results*?

sections.heading: A real dilemma, and the idea
sections.text: A pharmacist has one dose of a scarce drug and two patients who need it: a younger stranger likely to recover fully, and a longtime customer who is a friend. What should guide the choice? *Consequentialism* asks which action produces the best overall outcome. *Deontology* asks which duties and rights are in play, and whether any principle (like treating people equally) must hold regardless of outcome. *Virtue ethics* asks what a fair, compassionate, practically wise person would do, and what the choice reveals about character. None of these is a formula that spits out one answer; each highlights different features worth weighing.

sections.heading: Worked example: one case, three lenses
sections.text: Case: a manager can quietly cut corners on a safety test to hit a deadline, and no one would likely find out. Consequentialist lens: tally likely harms (risk to users, eroded trust) against benefits (on-time launch); the hidden low-probability catastrophe usually dominates. Deontological lens: cutting corners breaks a duty of honesty and treats users merely as means to a deadline — wrong even if undetected. Virtue lens: an honest, courageous professional would not become the kind of person who hides risks; the act corrodes integrity. Notice the lenses can converge, but for different reasons.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For each, name the framework doing the reasoning: (1) 'It'll cause more suffering than happiness overall.' (2) 'You promised — a promise is a duty.' (3) 'A generous person simply wouldn't do that.' (4) 'The rule must apply to everyone equally, whatever the result.' (5) 'The outcome with the most well-being wins.' Model answers: 1-consequentialism, 2-deontology, 3-virtue ethics, 4-deontology, 5-consequentialism.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking one framework is simply 'correct' and the others are errors — each captures real moral considerations. Mistake: treating consequentialism as 'the ends justify any means' caricature; most versions weigh *all* consequences, including broken trust. Exit: (a) Which framework centers duties and rights? (b) Which centers character? Answers: deontology; virtue ethics.

lessons.title: Bioethics and medical dilemmas
lessons.grammar_note: Four familiar bioethics principles: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the core principles of bioethics and apply the three frameworks to a medical case. Warm-up: what does a patient's *autonomy* protect?

sections.heading: A real dilemma, and the idea
sections.text: A competent adult patient refuses a blood transfusion that would very likely save her life, citing sincere personal convictions. The team believes the transfusion is clearly in her medical interest. Bioethics often organizes such cases around four principles: *autonomy* (respect informed choices), *beneficence* (do good), *non-maleficence* (avoid harm), and *justice* (distribute care fairly). Here autonomy and beneficence pull in opposite directions, which is exactly what makes it a dilemma rather than a math problem.

sections.heading: Worked example: one case, three lenses
sections.text: Case above, analyzed. Consequentialist lens: compare outcomes — overriding her may save a life but sets a precedent that erodes trust in medicine and treats patients as passive; respecting refusal risks her death but preserves a system patients can trust. Deontological lens: forcing treatment violates a duty to respect an informed, competent person's right over her own body — using her body against her will. Virtue lens: a wise, humane clinician respects the patient while ensuring the choice is genuinely informed and free of coercion. Many ethicists conclude that respecting a competent refusal is right — but the frameworks reach it by different routes, and reasonable people weigh the risk to life differently.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Identify the principle most in tension in each: (1) rationing scarce ICU beds during a surge; (2) a surgeon downplaying risks to 'reassure' a patient; (3) enrolling someone in a trial without full disclosure; (4) offering an experimental drug that might help but might harm. Model answers: 1-justice, 2-autonomy (informed consent), 3-autonomy, 4-beneficence vs. non-maleficence.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming 'the doctor knows best' settles every case — expertise about outcomes doesn't by itself override a patient's right to decide. Mistake: treating autonomy as absolute, ignoring justice when resources are shared. Exit: (a) Which principle protects informed patient choice? (b) Which principle governs fair distribution of scarce care? Answers: autonomy; justice.

lessons.title: Business and professional ethics
lessons.grammar_note: Ask: to whom does a professional owe duties — and what happens when those duties conflict?

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Analyze a workplace dilemma using stakeholders and the three frameworks. Warm-up: name two parties a company might owe something to.

sections.heading: A real dilemma, and the idea
sections.text: An engineer discovers her company's product has a defect that is unlikely, but could seriously injure a few users. Management wants to ship on schedule and disclose nothing. Should she stay quiet, push internally, or blow the whistle publicly? Business ethics often maps the *stakeholders* — customers, employees, shareholders, the public — and asks what is owed to each. Professionals also carry role-specific duties (an engineer's duty to safety, an accountant's to honest books) that can clash with an employer's wishes.

sections.heading: Worked example: one case, three lenses
sections.text: The defect case, analyzed. Consequentialist lens: weigh expected harm to users and long-term reputational damage against short-term costs of delay; low-probability severe harm plus lost trust usually outweighs hitting a date. Deontological lens: there is a duty not to deceive customers and to respect their right to know about risks they're exposed to. Virtue lens: an honest, courageous professional voices the concern and escalates responsibly, while practical wisdom counsels trying internal channels before going public. The frameworks broadly agree the silence is wrong, but they disagree about *how far* she must go and at what personal cost.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For each, name the stakeholder most affected and one framework that flags a problem: (1) padding an expense report; (2) targeting a manipulative ad at vulnerable users; (3) hiding a conflict of interest from a client; (4) laying off staff to boost a short-term stock price. Model answers: 1-employer/shareholders, deontology (honesty); 2-customers, consequentialism/virtue (harm, manipulation); 3-client, deontology (fiduciary duty); 4-employees vs. shareholders, consequentialism (whose welfare counts).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming 'it's legal' equals 'it's ethical' — law sets a floor, not the ceiling. Mistake: treating 'maximize shareholder value' as the only duty, ignoring other stakeholders. Exit: (a) Name one role-specific duty an engineer carries. (b) Does legality guarantee ethical acceptability? Answers: a duty to user safety (or honesty about risks); no.

questions.prompt: Judging an act by whether it maximizes overall well-being is characteristic of…
questions.explanation: Consequentialism evaluates outcomes.

questions.prompt: 'Never treat a person merely as a means' is a slogan most associated with…
questions.explanation: It reflects Kant's deontological respect for persons.

questions.prompt: A patient's right to refuse treatment rests mainly on the principle of…
questions.explanation: Autonomy protects informed, competent choice.

questions.prompt: Deciding how to allocate scarce ICU beds is primarily a question of…
questions.explanation: Justice concerns fair distribution.

questions.prompt: In business ethics, 'stakeholders' refers to…
options: all parties affected by a company's actions
questions.explanation: Stakeholders include customers, employees, shareholders, and the public.

questions.prompt: Which claim is a mistake in reasoning?
options: Legal acts can still be unethical
Frameworks can converge for different reasons
If it's legal, it must be ethical
questions.explanation: Legality is a floor, not proof of ethical acceptability.

lessons.title: Technology and AI ethics
lessons.grammar_note: Two recurring worries: what systems *know* about us (privacy) and how they *decide* about us (bias).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain privacy and algorithmic bias, and analyze an AI decision through the three frameworks. Warm-up: what does 'algorithmic bias' mean in one sentence?

sections.heading: A real dilemma, and the idea
sections.text: A bank deploys an AI model to screen loan applications. It is accurate on average, but it approves qualified applicants from one neighborhood at a noticeably lower rate — because it learned from historical data shaped by past discrimination. No one intended this. Two issues recur in tech ethics: *privacy* (what data is collected, and whether people meaningfully consent) and *algorithmic bias* (systems producing unfair outcomes for some groups, often by inheriting patterns in their training data).

sections.heading: Worked example: one case, three lenses
sections.text: The loan model, analyzed. Consequentialist lens: the system is efficient overall, but the concentrated harm to a disadvantaged group — and the wider erosion of trust — can outweigh the average gain. Deontological lens: treating similar applicants differently by neighborhood can violate a duty of equal treatment and a right against unjust discrimination, regardless of efficiency. Virtue lens: a just and honest institution audits its systems, explains its decisions, and does not hide behind 'the algorithm decided.' A subtle point: because the bias is unintended, blame and responsibility come apart — the outcome is unfair even though no individual set out to be unfair, which raises the question of who must fix it.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Label each as mainly a *privacy* or *bias* concern, and name one framework it engages: (1) an app selling location data without clear consent; (2) a hiring tool that downgrades one group's résumés; (3) facial recognition that misidentifies some faces far more often; (4) a service quietly recording conversations. Model answers: 1-privacy, deontology (consent/rights); 2-bias, deontology/consequentialism (unequal treatment, harm); 3-bias, justice/consequentialism; 4-privacy, deontology (autonomy).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a system is neutral because 'it's just math' — models can encode the biases of their data. Mistake: treating 'I clicked accept' as full, meaningful consent when terms are unreadable. Exit: (a) Where does algorithmic bias often come from? (b) Can an unfair outcome occur without anyone intending it? Answers: biased or skewed training data (and design choices); yes.

lessons.title: Environmental ethics
lessons.grammar_note: Key split: does nature matter only for human use (instrumental) or also in itself (intrinsic)?

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish instrumental from intrinsic value and apply the frameworks to an environmental trade-off. Warm-up: name someone affected by today's pollution who cannot vote today.

sections.heading: A real dilemma, and the idea
sections.text: A town can approve a factory that brings jobs and cheaper goods now, but will pollute a river and warm the local climate for decades. Environmental ethics asks *whose interests count*: present people, future generations, non-human animals, ecosystems themselves? A central question is whether nature has only *instrumental* value (useful to humans) or also *intrinsic* value (worth protecting for its own sake). How you answer changes what the trade-off even is.

sections.heading: Worked example: one case, three lenses
sections.text: The factory, analyzed. Consequentialist lens: sum benefits and harms — but *over what time frame and for whom?* Including future generations and ecological damage often flips a short-term 'net positive' into a long-term loss. Deontological lens: we may owe duties to future people not to hand them a degraded world, and possibly duties regarding animals and ecosystems, independent of our own gains. Virtue lens: a temperate, far-sighted community practices stewardship rather than short-term greed. Reasonable people disagree about how much to weigh distant, uncertain futures against pressing present needs like jobs — that disagreement is where the real argument lives.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For each, name whether it appeals to *intrinsic* or *instrumental* value: (1) 'Protect the wetland because it filters our drinking water.' (2) 'The old-growth forest matters even if no human ever visits it.' (3) 'Save the bees because we need them for crops.' (4) 'This species has worth in its own right.' Model answers: 1-instrumental, 2-intrinsic, 3-instrumental, 4-intrinsic.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming environmental ethics ignores human needs — the hard cases are precisely where jobs and health both matter. Mistake: treating 'future generations' as automatically outweighing everyone, or as counting for nothing. Exit: (a) Define intrinsic value in a phrase. (b) Name one party in these cases who cannot represent themselves in today's decision. Answers: worth for its own sake, not just usefulness; future generations (or non-human animals).

items.translation: the view that an action's rightness depends on its outcomes
items.example: By consequentialism, the option producing the most overall well-being is favored.

items.translation: the view that rightness depends on duties, rules, and rights rather than outcomes
items.example: Deontology can forbid a lie even when it would produce good results.

items.translation: the view that ethics centers on good character and what a virtuous person would do
items.example: Virtue ethics asks whether an act reflects honesty, courage, and practical wisdom.

items.translation: a person's right to make informed decisions about their own life and body
items.example: Respecting autonomy means honoring a competent patient's informed refusal.

items.translation: systematic unfairness in a computer system's outputs, often inherited from its data
items.example: Algorithmic bias let the model approve one group's loans less often.

items.translation: worth that something has in itself, not merely as a means to something else
items.example: Some argue a wilderness has intrinsic value beyond its usefulness to people.

questions.prompt: Algorithmic bias most often originates in…
options: skewed training data and design choices
questions.explanation: Models can inherit patterns in the data they learn from.

questions.prompt: Valuing a forest 'for its own sake' expresses…
questions.explanation: Intrinsic value is worth in itself.

questions.prompt: Rawls's 'veil of ignorance' asks you to choose rules without knowing…
options: which position in society you'll occupy
questions.explanation: Not knowing your place models impartial fairness.

questions.prompt: An unfair outcome produced by an AI that no one intended shows that…
options: responsibility and blame can come apart from a bad outcome
ethics does not apply to machines
questions.explanation: Outcomes can be unjust even absent bad intent, raising who must fix them.

questions.prompt: Concern over an app collecting data without meaningful consent is primarily about…
questions.explanation: Privacy concerns what is collected and whether consent is real.

questions.prompt: Which best reflects a virtue-ethics question?
options: What would a person of good character do here?
questions.explanation: Virtue ethics foregrounds character and practical wisdom.

lessons.title: Applied project: analyze a real dilemma

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose one real ethical dilemma — from medicine, business, technology, or the environment — that you find genuinely hard (a case where thoughtful people disagree). Write a short analysis that runs it through all three frameworks. Your goal is not to preach a verdict but to reason carefully and show your work.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State the dilemma in two or three sentences, including who is affected. 2) Analyze it through the consequentialist lens (weigh outcomes for everyone involved, over an honest time frame). 3) Analyze it through the deontological lens (name the duties and rights in play). 4) Analyze it through the virtue lens (what would a person of good character do, and why). 5) Apply one fairness test — e.g., Rawls's veil of ignorance: would you accept the outcome not knowing which party you'd be? 6) State your tentative conclusion and the strongest objection to it.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ The dilemma is genuinely contested, not a case with an obvious answer. ✔ Each framework is applied accurately and does real work (you'd notice if one were removed). ✔ You represented the opposing view fairly before disagreeing with it. ✔ Your conclusion is tentative and names its strongest objection. If all four hold, you've reasoned like an ethicist — presenting the frameworks, then thinking for yourself.
